The world has a distorted view of health. We have lost the compass that was meant to show us the right balance. We tend to swing from one extreme to another: from medicines to herbs, from surgery to energy massages. We have lost sight of the basic principles that our Creator gave us in the operating manual for human beings, the Bible. Although some individuals mix health and religion to the point of becoming fanatics, the biblical principles governing health are important, remarkably balanced and still practical today!

Why be in good health?

The question then arises: why be in good health? Why do you want to be healthy? Why must you be? Why does God care about it? Simply because it is essential. Our body is the means that allows us to live a meaningful life and to accomplish what we came to do on earth.

The Bible is not a treatise on health or dietetics. However, in the Scriptures, God gives basic principles to guide our personal choices so that we can enjoy good health and escape disease. In the Bible God revealed fundamental truths that medical science took many centuries to confirm.

Spiritual health and physical health

One of the most interesting advances in the field of health is the recognition of what is called “mental and spiritual health.” This field admits the important role that beliefs and values play in behavior and health. And you who are reading are a believer. So put to work what you have in order to be in good health and live long.

“My son, […] let your heart keep my commandments; for they will add to you length of days, years of life, and peace.” (Prov 3:1-2)

What are these commandments? Here are a few:

“Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight. Don’t be wise in your own eyes. Fear Yahweh, and depart from evil. It will be health to your body, and nourishment to your bones. Honor Yahweh with your substance, with the first fruits of all your increase: so your barns will be filled with plenty, and your vats will overflow with new wine.” (Prov 3:5-10)

Inner rest

Before observing any rules about food, sport and many other things, you must start by putting yourself at rest on the inside. These verses highlight certain factors you probably don’t think about, but which will keep you in good health: tranquility, trust in God, integrity, humility and generosity. All of this will allow you to enjoy better health, because your spiritual health has an influence on your physical health.

Are you calm inside? Aren’t you overwhelmed by worry and agitation? It is true that you have to make ends meet, as the saying goes. What if you let God take care of making them meet while you do what is your part: working peacefully (2 Thess 3:12), thinking things through with trust in God (Prov 16:20) and praying with thanksgiving (Phil 4:6)? Knowing how much harm worries and agitation can do us, the Lord Jesus Christ instructs us:

“Therefore I tell you, don’t be anxious for your life, what you will eat, nor yet for your body, what you will wear. […] Don’t seek what you will eat or what you will drink; neither be anxious. For the nations of the world seek after all of these things, but your Father knows that you need these things.” (Luke 12:22, 29-30)

“Casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.” (1 Pet 5:7)

“In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.” (Phil 4:6-7)

Instead of staying worried about what you don’t have and the challenges to face, thank God for his presence with you and in you. Thank him for the things you already have, and thank him for the challenges that lie ahead of you, with confidence that God will help you meet them with honor. And think of visiting and helping someone.

Putting joy on someone’s face increases your joy and your inner peace. Indeed, it is the Holy Spirit who rejoices in you. God is pleased with you. Jehovah Rapha is pleased with you. The result will be the fulfillment of his promise: “You shall serve Yahweh your God, and he will bless your bread and your water, and I will take sickness away from among you. No one will miscarry or be barren in your land. I will fulfill the number of your days.” (Exod 23:25-26)

Clean and unclean meats

The Bible distinguishes between clean and unclean animals to eat. But does God really care which meats we eat? It goes without saying. If he wants us to be in good health, then he cares about what we eat, down to the details. Jesus declares: “Or who is there among you, who, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, who will give him a serpent? If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!” (Matt 7:9-11)

Like any human father who wants his children to enjoy the best things in life and who cares about giving them good food to eat, our heavenly Father wishes to offer us everything that is best. Our elders teach us how to live, but our heavenly Father also has something to say about what is good for us and what is not, including the meats unfit for our consumption. God defines which meats are fit or unfit for consumption.

a) Beyond the law

Our Creator has given us a list of “clean” meats, fit for consumption, and so-called “unclean” meats, that is, unfit for consumption, in the 11th chapter of Leviticus and in the 14th chapter of Deuteronomy. These are the instructions of the Lord to Israel in the time of Moses. But in fact, these directives go back to an earlier time: Noah already knew, before the flood, the distinction between clean and unclean animals (Gen 7:2).

b) Definition

God explains that for a fish to be “clean” — that is, edible — it must have scales and fins. This is the case, for example, with sea bass, cod, flounder, grouper, salmon, snapper, trout, mackerel, sardine, tuna and other fish in this category. On the other hand, catfish, lobster, crab, shrimp, eel and many other sea creatures — including shellfish — having neither fins nor scales, are unfit for consumption and “unclean.”

The so-called “clean” land animals are those with a divided hoof that chew the cud. Belonging to this category, for example, are cattle, goat, sheep, elk, deer and antelope. On the other hand, the rabbit, the horse and the pig are not “clean”; they are not edible. God did not create them to be eaten.

In Deut 14:11-18, there is a list of birds unfit for consumption such as the eagle, vulture, buzzard, falcon, raven, ostrich, owl, seagull, hawk, stork and heron. Since the chicken, turkey, duck, goose, quail and pheasant do not appear on this list of unclean birds, they are “clean,” that is, good to eat.

Most insects are not good to eat, but God says that some of them, such as locusts, grasshoppers and crickets, are edible (Lev 11:22).

c) Why?

People sometimes wonder why God declared certain animals fit for human consumption and others not. If we must speak in biblical terms, it would be better to keep silent. God declares that he is holy and wants us to be holy (Lev 11:45; 20:7), we his sons and daughters (2 Cor 6:17-18). Passages such as John 1:12 and John 20:17, as well as several other passages of Scripture, confirm this idea. Our Father wants all of us, men and women, to be like him — holy and pure.

If that were all there was to it, one wonders why the apostles, when giving instructions on holiness to Christians, did not stress the question of clean and unclean animals. We see rather the opposite. The apostle Paul says: “I know, and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus, that nothing is unclean of itself; except that to him who considers anything to be unclean, to him it is unclean.” (Rom 14:14)

But this is no reason to encourage eating these creatures without a little thought. Many dietitians and health experts point out the benefits for our health of avoiding the foods the Bible calls unclean, even if they do not use this terminology. It must be admitted that with modern cooking methods, many risks of contamination by bacteria can be avoided. But the debates on this last point are still heated.

As Christians, we are freed from the ceremonial form of sanctification. Eating so-called clean or unclean animals therefore does not affect our relationship with God in any way. It is not a food that brings us closer to God: if we eat, we have nothing more; if we don’t eat, we have nothing less (1 Cor 8:8). For the kingdom of God is not eating and drinking, but righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit (Rom 14:17).

That being the case, the Christian is free to eat what he wants. But since scientists recognize that there are risks in consuming these animals, it is fitting to avoid them or to reduce their consumption as much as possible.

The biblical dietary laws

The Bible contains other important instructions that medical science has only understood very recently.

a) No blood and no visible fat in the diet

Divinely inspired, Moses reports that blood and fat, even from clean animals, must not be part of the human diet (Lev 3:17; 7:23-26; Gen 9:4). Animal blood can contain bacteria and viruses that are transmissible. This important biblical prohibition aims to prevent the spread of disease.

The prohibition on eating visible fat is also important. One of the most interesting discoveries of the epidemiological studies carried out over the last fifty years has been the link between sustained fat consumption and heart disease, strokes and various types of cancer. These diseases lead to death in regions where people eat a lot of fatty foods. Many ordinary foods can contain more than 50% fat. In our modern society, a very fatty, high-calorie diet leads to weight problems. Medical science has learned that eating fat is dangerous — whereas God had already revealed it to Moses thousands of years earlier!

b) More fruits, vegetables and grains

In Genesis, we read that God had given human beings fruits, vegetables and grains for food (Gen 1:29; 2:16; 9:3). Fruits, vegetables and all grains contain fiber and other carbohydrates. Fiber plays an important role in the intestines and has an important place in protecting the body against colon cancer and other chronic diseases. Complex carbohydrates are also necessary in a diet, because they lower the cholesterol level to prevent heart disease and strokes.

Serious health problems are the result of eating too many refined carbohydrates. Refined sugar and flour have been emptied of their nutritional content. Populations that consume large quantities of refined carbohydrates are among those with a very high rate of diabetes and similar problems. Yet the Bible warns us against this kind of diet. Solomon was divinely inspired to say: “It is not good to eat much honey” (see Prov 25:16, 27). Even though honey is a “natural” substance, it is “refined” in a sense by the bees that produce it. The pollen collected from a large number of flowers is found in concentrated form in certain honeys. The biblical principle is to consume refined carbohydrates in moderation. However, because of the craze for soft drinks, pastries, sweets and sugary food, many people take in more than 45 kilograms (about 100 pounds) of refined sugar a year — to the detriment of their health!

When these biblical instructions are analyzed objectively, they confirm the conclusions of the latest research in dietetics: reduce the consumption of fats, increase the use of complex carbohydrates (fruits, vegetables and all grains), limit the consumption of refined dishes and carbohydrates. Most human beings suffering from disease could have been spared if they had observed God’s instructions!

c) Vegetarianism is not biblical

Some believe that human beings should not eat meat. Pagan philosophers and many others in the East spread ideas about vegetarianism in the ancient world. Some say that, since the Scriptures do not specifically mention that God gave meat to Adam and Eve to eat, it should not be eaten. This forgets that God — the Author of the laws on clean and unclean meats — said: “These are the animals which you may eat” (Deut 14:4). Abraham also served a meal to two angels and to the One who became the Jesus Christ of the New Testament (Gen 18:3). This meal consisted of cakes, meat, butter and milk (Gen 18:6-8). Jesus Christ served fish to his disciples (John 21:9-13). The apostle Paul warned New Testament Christians not to let themselves be seduced by vegetarianism (Rom 14:2; 1 Tim 4:3). In dietetics, the Bible helps us find the balanced position between extreme opinions.

Alcohol and drug abuse

The Bible clearly condemns drunkenness and alcohol abuse (Prov 20:1; 1 Cor 5:11), but it approves of its use on many occasions (Deut 14:26; Matt 26:29). Jesus changed water into wine at a wedding (John 2:1-11). Paul recommended the use of wine for health: “use a little wine for your stomach’s sake and your frequent infirmities” (1 Tim 5:23). The key is moderation (Phil 4:5). A moderate amount of alcohol helps relaxation, reduces the risk of cardiovascular disease and increases the amount of gastric acid, which aids digestion in people who are starting to get older. The Bible provides important advice on using alcohol, but it requires personal decisions that develop individual character!

If you have decided to avoid alcoholic drink completely, you are not wrong; quite the contrary. Paul’s recommendation to Timothy is for a personal health reason. Moreover, the context shows that Timothy did not drink alcohol at all. And Paul did not blame him for that. On the contrary, when he gave him the recommendation, he felt obliged to justify himself, which the apostle does not usually do. Furthermore, Paul never said that he used wine regularly and encouraged every Christian to do so. If you have enough discipline to approach alcoholic drinks without becoming their slave, you are free to do so. Otherwise, stay away from them. There is enough alcohol in other foods to meet your body’s needs.

Although tobacco and drugs are not mentioned in the Scriptures, the principles that guide the use of such substances are clearly set out there. Your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Cor 6:19) and “If anyone destroys God’s temple [the human body], God will destroy him” (1 Cor 3:17). The Bible declares, without a shadow of a doubt, that we must not damage our body — which is what drugs do (whether legal or not).

These biblical principles are preventive in nature; anyone with common sense will easily notice it. Dependence on alcohol, tobacco or drugs is a kind of idolatry and covetousness — a violation of several divine commandments. The biblical principles of health are not meant to curb the pleasure we can enjoy, but they were given to make sure that these pleasures are positive and beneficial.

Physical exercise

The apostle Paul also advised it, although our priority must be on spiritual things: “bodily exercise has some value” (1 Tim 4:8). This is exactly what current research has shown. Exercise must be done regularly, because its effects are only temporary! However, these effects are important: they reduce the cholesterol level, blood pressure and stress, and they prevent diabetes, heart disease and a host of other problems. It seems to me that Jesus never held a sports session with his disciples. That is because they did it almost constantly. They walked long distances every day, they moved around, they got enough physical activity. This physically active lifestyle keeps us in good health and gives us the endurance we need to accomplish our mission.

Rest

“Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. You shall labor six days, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God. You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates.” (Exod 20:8-10)

Whatever work demands your attention, rest is essential and obligatory. If you want to work well, start by resting well. With good rest, your physical strength will be renewed, but your spiritual, supernatural strength, which comes from the Lord, will also be renewed. That, moreover, is the most important rest.

In Matt 11:28-29, Jesus did not say: “Come and I will give you riches, or even power, or anything else.” But he spoke first of rest, the rest of the soul. It is the most important, the dearest rest. It is a rest that accompanies you every day and in all circumstances. He gives it to us when we come to him, but we maintain it when we follow his instructions. When we obey the Lord and agree to carry our cross following him, paradoxically to what a cross that is carried brings, we have rest, that rest which comes from God alone.

Conclusion: seven keys to perfect health

If we put together everything that precedes, we will see that the Bible (as well as medical science) shows us the following seven keys to guarantee perfect health.

  1. Trust in God. This banishes the worry and inner agitation that do more damage than they advance our life.
  2. Define your values, which will be precious guides for you throughout your journey with regard to your health. One example: never eat late (after 10 p.m.).
  3. Eat real. Eat whole, unprocessed foods, and respect the biblical dietary rules.
  4. Move. We are made to move. So seize every opportunity to do so: walk, ride a bike, take the stairs, garden, tinker, park far away, get off two bus stops before your destination, and so on. These small daily things count far more than a sporting effort once a week!
  5. Rest. In our overcharged society, this is one of the hardest things to achieve. We run, we are going at 200 miles an hour. There is always something to do, to experience, and we rarely give ourselves time to regenerate, to rest or to watch the clouds go by. We even cut short our sleep for activities that aren’t worth it. Have you ever stayed up late to finish a movie, play a game or be on social media?
  6. Learn to say no. Saying no to what is not essential will allow you to manage your health better.
  7. Stay connected to God. This gives you the spiritual strength and peace needed to maintain all the other principles.

Money and you

Money is part of your life. If you do not master your finances, your life will be scattered. It is not about being rich. It is about controlling yourself financially. Sources of income are generally not very numerous. But never dare to say the same about expenses. You must spend on many things that are obligatory. We can mention: housing costs (rent, property taxes, maintenance, furniture, etc.), utilities, food, clothing, transport, insurance, health costs, savings (emergency fund, education fund, retirement fund, etc.). It is essential to put money aside regularly. This helps develop discipline, fights covetousness and materialism, and provides for future needs. You must also count: debt repayment, leisure (if possible, even in modest amounts), helping the needy (generosity is a divine principle) and miscellaneous (you probably haven’t thought of everything).

To manage all this well, you need real control over these financial flows, but also and above all over yourself when it comes to money. You need to have financial control of yourself. What direction does your attitude take when a large sum of money falls into your hands? Generally, an excitement is born inside. Managing this excitement is what I mean by financial self-control. What lies at the origin of this excitement is the insatiable consuming element in man. Ecclesiastes knows something about it: “All the labor of man is for his mouth, and yet the appetite is not filled.” (Eccl 6:7)

This consuming element is in fact the old man. It is the serpent’s tongue. It is insatiable. It is ready to eat the forbidden. It wants to devour the garden instead of cultivating it. It is the source of the excitement. It dances because there is something to devour. You must be very careful, otherwise you will eat the forbidden and end up among the poorest. Your attitude toward money must be such that the flow of money coming into and going out of your pocket does not control your emotions. We often pray that money would not be our master. Well, in addition to prayer, we must act:

Rename your work

Do not consider it a mere breadwinner anymore. The following verse shows what the Bible thinks of your economic activity: “Let him who stole steal no more; but rather let him labor, producing with his hands something that is good, that he may have something to give to him who has need.” (Eph 4:28)

Your work, your business is a source of income. It is a channel for accumulating resources. And these resources must be well distributed, with generosity as the priority.

Redefine your source

We call our economic activities sources of income. But we must look further in our definitions of the source of our resources. God is the source of everything. He is our source. If we manage to live by this thought, we will no longer be hooked on our work, job or business. And we will no longer be at the mercy of everyone who jingles a few coins. God is our source. He is neither unable nor stingy. On the contrary: “God is able to make all grace abound to you, that you, always having all sufficiency in everything, may abound to every good work.” (2 Cor 9:8)

Never wait for money

If you wait for it, you will become dependent on it. On the contrary, think, imagine, find ideas, project, plan, determine the necessary resources, then reach out and take those resources to invest. If you wait for money before being objective and precise in your ideas, you never will be. You must not wait for money because it is not your master.

Generosity

When you meet an economist, the first thing he will talk to you about is the management strategy beginning with the words savings, investment and budget. What he simply wants to make you understand is that you must be smart enough to multiply your money. He is right. Only, the best way to multiply your money, according to God, is this one word: give.

“Give, and it will be given to you: good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over, will be given to you. For with the same measure you measure it will be measured back to you.” (Luke 6:38)

“A man’s gift makes room for him, and brings him before great men.” (Prov 18:16)

“Cast your bread on the waters; for you shall find it after many days. Give a portion to seven, yes, even to eight; for you don’t know what evil will be on the earth.” (Eccl 11:1-2)

“There is one who scatters, and increases yet more. There is one who withholds more than is appropriate, but gains poverty. The liberal soul shall be made fat. He who waters shall be watered also himself.” (Prov 11:24-25)

Make giving a habit

Give generously to individuals, not only your relatives, but also strangers. “Don’t forget to show hospitality to strangers, for in doing so, some have entertained angels without knowing it.” (Heb 13:2)

It is also necessary that you structure your generosity. You are a steward of the goods God has given you and will have to give an account. So structure your generosity.

From all your income, pay the tithe in the congregation where you are fed by the word and spiritually cared for. Forget the arguments against the tithe and do not get carried away by how it is managed. All those who have practiced the tithe with faith testify positively to it. Obey God in this area and expect your reward.

Also give offerings to contribute to God’s work in your Christian community and to support the ministers of God whom he uses to add to your faith. “But let him who is taught in the word share all good things with him who teaches.” (Gal 6:6)

In any case, let the Holy Spirit lead you in your decisions about what to give, where, how and to whom.

Invest

Put your money to work and stop working for money. When you manage to invest money, you secure income that will no longer cost you much time and energy. And generally, this income is more abundant than what we get from our hard work. So it is good that you think about investing and that you do it. In any case, biblical wisdom strongly urges us to. To insist, it uses images:

“He called ten servants of his and gave them ten mina coins, and told them, ‘Conduct business until I come.’” (Luke 19:13)

“But he who received the one talent went away and dug in the earth, and hid his lord’s money. […] But his lord answered him, ‘You wicked and slothful servant. You knew that I reap where I didn’t sow, and gather where I didn’t scatter. You ought therefore to have deposited my money with the bankers, and at my coming I should have received back my own with interest. Take away therefore the talent from him, and give it to him who has the ten talents. For to everyone who has will be given, and he will have abundance, but from him who doesn’t have, even that which he has will be taken away.’” (Matt 25:18, 26-29)

“She (the virtuous woman) considers a field, and buys it. With the fruit of her hands, she plants a vineyard.” (Prov 31:16)

Obviously, investing is a worry when you have no accumulated resources. Well, this can easily be solved. The key is savings. Whatever your current financial situation, you can save. When you have finished setting aside your tithe from your income, think of yourself. Put a dividend for yourself into a savings account and forget about it. Then live on the rest. If it is not enough, do not think about what you have saved. Ask God and knock on other doors. Continue like this until you have something substantial to invest. Pray and place it strategically. Follow the Holy Spirit in your investment and soon money will run after you.

A short note on savings: Choose carefully where you save. Do not allow a dishonest individual to run off with your fortune. Also, do not become stingy for this reason. You must take care of yourself and you must keep exercising generosity. And do not invest in anything that tends to impoverish the needy even more. You will not be able to enjoy it. “He who increases his wealth by excessive interest gathers it for one who has pity on the poor.” (Prov 28:8)

Get out of debt

Do you have debts? If you do not, then glory to God. Do not read this chapter, unless to help someone else. You need to get out of debt, otherwise money and its properties will be your masters. “The rich rule over the poor. The borrower is servant to the lender.” (Prov 22:7)

God does not want you to be a slave in any way. Have you ever heard of financial freedom? The only one who truly wants it for you is God. Because: “No servant can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to one, and despise the other. You aren’t able to serve God and Mammon.” (Luke 16:13)

God wants your worship. And he wants it in a singular way. That is why providing for your subsistence is his priority. Do not let the religious deceive you. God makes it rain and the sun rise on the good and the wicked. He grants us fruitful seasons and fills our barns. This is how he bears witness to all of his nature, calling them to receive eternal and abundant life in Jesus Christ. And now that you are a child of God, providing for your needs is his priority. So, start getting out of debt by taking the resources God puts at your disposal (Deut 15:6; Prov 6:1-5).

Believe in God’s promise

He watches over his word to fulfill it. He said he will bless all your activities by pouring great abundance into them. He said he would ensure your subsistence. He promised to see to it that you always have what you need and that you are dependent on no one. All this is true. God holds firm. So believe these words. Declare them constantly over your life and your circumstances.

Stop taking new loans

Live on what you have. Live at your current income level.

Come to an agreement with your creditors

Go and see them after praying. Tell them how you can settle according to your current income. Forget the old agreements. You have the right to ask again. You can only do what your means allow. Forget the laws, whatever they are. For the moment, the only rule that matters is that you live. You are not going to kill yourself to settle debts. Worry is not the solution. Get that into your head. Then, pray. And go and meet your creditors to ask for new agreements. But you are not going to talk to them about your right to live. That concerns only you. Instead, you will plead with them until they yield. And this will happen because God is with you. When the Lord approves a man’s ways, he makes even his enemies be at peace with him (Prov 16:7).

Pay

Whoever pays his debts grows rich. Strive to settle your debt. Do it drop by drop. But make sure you do it all the same. If there is someone who borrows and does not repay, it is the wicked. And it is certainly not you.

Live on a budget

Count as precisely as possible what you will have consumed on your food, travel, clothing, housing and other costs related to your subsistence over one month. If you do this, you will know how much you cost yourself. And if you compare that with your work, you will realize the enormity of God’s grace toward you. You will also realize that you are probably already eating your seed (means of investment). You will also understand that you must reorient your financial habits and structure your finances. And above all, you will know with certainty how you must do this structuring. The latter is what economists call budgeting. The Bible agrees as well. It speaks of it in a figurative way (Prov 27:23-27; Prov 21:5).

The general rules of budgeting do not apply to all living conditions. So you must study your case in the manner explained above. That way, you will know which of the following rules you must apply and how you must do it. Following a budget amounts to doing the following things:

  • Draw up a list of all expenses
  • Rank needs in order of priority
  • Say “No!” to non-essential things
  • Estimate, realistically, the available resources
  • Decide how to distribute resources according to the level of priority
  • Take the steps you can so as not to spend more than you have

Some of our needs are future needs; this requires discipline, because we must not spend everything we have now but rather save for the future. It can be difficult, but learning to say “No!” can considerably help rebalance your budget and help you get out of excessive debt. Anything that is not part of the budget should not be spent.

Setting up a budget and sticking to it often includes some faith and action. There are situations where even our best plans, on paper, in our budget, seem unachievable. It happens. We must do our best — fulfill our tasks — and lean on God with faith, so that he makes up for our shortcomings.

We are not masters of the future (even though we should draw up a realistic budget). It is true that “man proposes, but God disposes” (read Prov 19:21; Jas 4:13-15; Eccl 9:11).

lecons.titre: Mastering your money — When money does not come in regularly
lecons.html:
Everything we have said before assumes that money comes in, more or less every month. But perhaps, among those who read this manual, there are some who live something else. Their money arrives by surprise: a small contract, then nothing for weeks. What they earn is not even always enough for the needs of the moment. So they borrow to hold on. When a payment arrives, they repay. A few days later, they have nothing left, and they start again. If this is your life right now, this part is written for you.

First, one thing: this is not the end for you. What you are going through does not mean you have no faith, nor that you are lazy, nor that you are a failure. When money arrives by surprise, an ordinary budget cannot hold. You need a method made for your situation, not more shame.

See how it goes around

Look at how it happens. A payment arrives. Right away, it goes to debts and emergencies. Then comes the month when there is nothing. You borrow to eat. The next payment is used to repay that loan. And you fall back into lack. What must be broken is the loan taken in panic, when you are in a hurry and afraid.

Joseph shows us another path. Before the years without harvest, he advised setting aside a fifth of the harvest during the seven good years (Gen 41:34-36). Not everything: one fifth. People kept on living during the good years, and when the bad years came, there was food to eat. “The ants are not a strong people, yet they provide their food in the summer.” (Prov 30:25). Every payment that arrives is a small good year. What you keep from that payment will decide how you get through the difficult month.

Know two numbers

The first is your minimum to live on. It is the money you need each month to hold on: housing, food, transport to get to work, health, and the small expenses that cannot be avoided. Not comfort, not outings. It is not the amount you dream of. It is the amount below which you cannot go.

The second is what you earn on average per month. Take everything you earned during the last six months. Add it up. Then divide by six. Do not rely on the last big payment: it hides the truth about your situation.

Compare the two. If what you earn on average is greater than your minimum to live on, your problem is that the money arrives in fits and starts. The steps that follow are enough. If it is smaller, money is truly missing every month. In that case, you will also need to lower your expenses and bring in more money (see the last step). In both cases, you will finally know where you stand. You do not come out of the dark without turning on the light.

Give yourself a salary

When a payment arrives, do not spend it as it comes. Put it in a separate place: a separate account, a Mobile Money number that you keep only for this, or with a trusted person. Then give yourself the same amount every week, like a salary. To find it, take your minimum to live on and divide by four. This salary is your budget. When a big contract arrives, you no longer think yourself rich. When nothing arrives, you are no longer lost: your salary continues as long as there is money set aside. And when that money goes down, you see it coming and can act earlier.

Divide every incoming payment

When money arrives by surprise, a fixed amount (“I put 20,000 F aside each month”) does not hold. The month when there is nothing, you give up and feel guilty. Do it differently: every time money comes in, divide it the same way, whatever the amount. One part to give, one part to set aside, one part for debts, and the rest for your salary.

Here is an example. You receive 100,000 F. You give 10% as the tithe in your church: that is 10,000 F. You set aside 5%: that is 5,000 F. You keep 10% for debts: that is 10,000 F. There remains 75,000 F for your salary. (10% means 10 F out of every 100 F.) Even 5% set aside each time is already a good habit.

If what you earn on average is smaller than your minimum to live on, do not sacrifice food and housing to repay. Use very small percentages for the money set aside and for debts, and talk with those you owe money to, as we said above.

As for giving, do not let yourself be crushed. “For if the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what you have, not according to what you don’t have.” (2 Cor 8:12). This means that God looks at what you have, not at what you don’t have. Jesus saw a poor widow put two small coins as an offering in the Temple, and he said she had given more than all the others (Luke 21:1-4). Always give, according to what you receive, even if it is small. This keeps your heart free from the love of money.

Set money aside

Your first goal is small: set aside one week of salary, and do not touch it, except in a real emergency. Then two weeks, then one month. This may take several months, and that is normal. Every week of money set aside is a week when you will not need to borrow. It is this money that will one day give you the strength to say no to a loan. Keep it far from your hand (an account where you cannot withdraw right away, or a trusted person), because the excitement we spoke about earlier is waiting for you at every payment.

Prepare for the difficult month before it comes

The loan taken in panic arrives when fear decides in your place. So decide now, when you are calm, what you will do in the next difficult month. Write it on the worksheet given to you with this module. Here is what to do, in order:

  • Cut everything that is not obligatory. Keep only what you truly need. This is the time to say “No!”.
  • Look at what you can sell: an item you don’t use, a tool, or a small job you know how to do and can be paid for.
  • Ask early. A deposit from a client, an advance from your boss, a helping hand from a relative. Asking early and small is better than asking late and big.
  • Refuse loans that hide other loans. Never take a loan to pay another loan. Do not turn to those who charge very high rates (Prov 28:8).
  • As a last resort only, if there is truly nothing left to do in order to eat or to get care: borrow just what is needed, from someone you know, and write down how you will repay, according to what you really earn.

Do not stay alone

“Two are better than one, […] For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.” (Eccl 4:9-10). God never wanted his children to carry lack all by themselves (Deut 15:11; Gal 6:2). Two things to do:

  • Talk about your situation to the Alliance. The Grace Fund exists for emergency cases. It is managed by the Ministry of Welfare, Mutual Aid and Generosity (MBEL). Let it be known, and the steps provided in the Internal Regulations will be followed. Speaking early is not shameful; it is mutual aid.
  • Join or form a small interest-free mutual-aid tontine with a few trusted builders. Each puts in a small amount at regular intervals, and in turn one member receives the whole (or else a common fund is used to help in emergencies). Write down the rules, choose a manager, and let everyone be able to see the accounts. Remember the note on savings above: do not entrust your money to someone you are not sure of.

Bring in more money, and more regularly

Setting aside is not enough if what comes in is smaller than what you need. You must also act on what you earn. Remember that God is your source, and that the work of your hands is the channel (Eph 4:28). This does not excuse you from acting: it helps you hold on while you act. Three leads:

  • Bring your clients back. Offer every satisfied client a follow-up: maintenance, small monthly repairs, a monthly contract. A client who pays every month is worth more than ten surprise contracts.
  • Add a second job, even a small one, alongside the first, in a field you already know.
  • Learn to do something that sells. Ask for advice from the Ministry of Business and Finance (MAF), which helps builders in their projects to earn money.

An example (made-up story)

Sylvain is a tiler. Here is what he earned over the last six months: 120,000 F, 0, 45,000 F, 180,000 F, 0, 75,000 F. That makes 420,000 F in total. Divided by six, this gives 70,000 F per month on average. His minimum to live on is 80,000 F. He sees that he is short 10,000 F every month. His problem is not that he is poorly organized: money is truly missing.

So he acts on both sides. He lowers his minimum to live on to 72,000 F by cutting his transport and phone expenses. Then he offers two former clients a maintenance contract of 8,000 F per month each. What he earns on average rises to 86,000 F. Now he gives himself 18,000 F per week (72,000 divided by 4). He divides every incoming payment, and his first goal is to set aside one week of salary: 18,000 F.

None of this happens in a month. But for the first time, he no longer suffers the difficult month: he prepares for it. (The figures are only there to give an example.)

You will not get out of this circle in one month. But every week of money set aside, every well-made division, every client who comes back is a step gained. Climb step after step, and keep your eyes on the one who promised to take care of all your needs (Phil 4:19).

lecons.titre: Mastering your money — The bank and the account
lecons.html:
Why have an account?

Many people keep their money at home: in a bag, in a box, in a pocket. It is easy. It is also risky, because a theft, a fire or a flood is enough to make everything disappear. And there is a more discreet danger: the money you have at hand is the money you spend. We spoke earlier about the excitement that takes hold of you when a sum comes into your hands. An account puts a little distance between you and your money, and this distance protects you from yourself.

An account first serves to keep your money safe, and to set it aside without touching it right away. It also allows you to receive a salary or a payment without carrying it all on you, and to keep track of what comes in and what goes out. The day you ask for a loan or housing, it will prove your income: a bank rarely lends to someone it does not know.

In the parable of the talents, the master says to the lazy servant: “You ought therefore to have deposited my money with the bankers” (Matt 25:27). Jesus does not condemn the bank. He condemns the one who buries his money in a hole.

Where can you keep your money?

There are several places, and each has its strengths and weaknesses.

PlaceWhat it isGood to know
The bankAn approved institution supervised, at the regional level, by the Central Bank (BCEAO).It offers many services: card, transfers, checkbook, loans. Fees need watching. It is sometimes far from villages.
Microfinance (SFD, savings bank, savings cooperative)A small approved institution that receives savings and lends to people whom banks do not always accept.It is closer, the welcome is simpler, you can deposit small amounts. Its loans often cost more (we will come back to this).
Mobile MoneyAn account linked to your phone number (MTN, Moov, Celtiis).Very practical for sending, receiving and paying. It has limits. It is not made for keeping large sums for a long time.
The tontine or mutual-aid groupMoney entrusted among people who know each other.Everything rests on trust. No law protects you if the manager disappears.
The houseYour money is close to you.It is protected from nothing, and it is too easy to spend.

Before entrusting your money, check that the institution is approved. “Approved” means it has received official authorization to operate. Ask to see this authorization. For banks, the list is published by the Central Bank (BCEAO). An institution without approval does not protect you.

The main types of account

AccountWhat it is forGood to know
Current account (checking account)Everyday money: salary, expenses, transfers. It entitles you to a card and sometimes a checkbook.It earns little or nothing. There are account-keeping fees. Beware of overdrafts.
Savings account (passbook)Setting money aside.Withdrawals are often limited or slower: this helps you not touch it. It earns a small interest.
Term deposit accountLocking a sum for a fixed period (six months, one year…).The interest is generally better. Taking the money back before the date can be costly.
Business accountFor your activity or your company.It separates the company’s money from yours. The bank asks for the company’s papers.
Joint accountAn account for two, for example for a couple.Each person can withdraw everything. Do this only with a trusted person, after agreeing on the rules.

Interest is the small sum the institution pays you for keeping your money. When you borrow, it is the opposite: you are the one who pays interest. We will talk about it in the part on credit.

Opening an account: how it goes

Opening an account is not complicated. You choose the institution (we will get to that below), you go there with your documents, you fill in the form and you make the first deposit, if one is asked of you. Before signing, read the contract, called the “account agreement,” and ask questions about every word you do not understand. You leave with your RIB (the sheet bearing your account number), your card if you asked for one, and the explanations for using the account.

The documents required are generally a valid official ID, proof of address or a location plan of your house, and passport-size photos. Some institutions also ask for the birth certificate, proof of income (pay slip, employer’s certificate) or your tax number (IFU), and a minimum first deposit that is not the same everywhere. The list changes from one institution to another: stop by or call beforehand to ask for it. For a business account, the company’s papers are added (trade register, tax number), which we will discuss again in Module 14.

Warning. No honest agent asks you for money for himself in order to “speed up” the opening of your account. Refuse, and speak to the branch manager.

Fees: read the menu before ordering

“For which of you, desiring to build a tower, doesn’t first sit down and count the cost, to see if he has enough to complete it?” (Luke 14:28) A bank is not free. It makes money through fees: each seems small, but many come back every month. There are opening fees, then account-keeping fees, that is, what you pay every month or every quarter just to have the account. The bank card is paid for when issued, then every year. Withdrawals sometimes cost, especially at another bank’s ATMs or at the counter. Transfers, statements and SMS alerts also have their price.

Two fees hurt more than the others. The overdraft: if you spend more than you have, the bank advances the difference and makes you pay dearly for it (these are the “overdraft charges”). And the bounced check: if you sign a check without having the money to pay it, you pay a penalty.

Always ask for the list of rates in writing. A serious institution gives it to you without difficulty. Compare two or three before choosing.

How to choose

To choose, ask yourself a few simple questions. Is the institution approved? Is it close to your home or your work? An account that is too far away is not used. What are the fees per month and per year, and what is the minimum deposit? Can you follow your account on your phone, and is it linked to your Mobile Money? How are customers treated, and how long do you wait at the counter? Will it be able to help you later with a loan or a business account? And what do trusted people who have had their account there for a long time say about it?

Fill in the sheet at the end of this part with two institutions. You will quickly see the difference.

Using your account well

A few habits make all the difference. Two accounts are better than one: one for the month’s expenses, one for the money set aside. If possible, without a card for the second one, so as not to touch it by reflex. Look at your balance every week, keep your receipts, and read your statements every month, because that is where errors and thefts are spotted.

Do not let the overdraft become a habit: it costs a lot and it hides the true situation. Never write a check without having the money in the account. It is a serious offense, which can make you lose your checkbook and lead to prosecution.

Finally, keep your codes to yourself: the card code, the Mobile Money code, the codes received by SMS. Do not give them to anyone, not even to someone who says they are “from the bank.” A real bank never asks for your secret code. And note down somewhere the number to call to block your card in case of loss or theft.

Mobile Money: a good tool, with its limits

Mobile Money has changed the lives of many people. You send, receive and pay at any hour, from your phone, without going to the bank. According to the Central Bank’s rules, customers’ money must be set aside in a bank account, safe from the operator’s debts.

It nevertheless has its limits. There are ceilings, per transaction, per day and for the balance, which change depending on the operator and on your account’s verification level: ask your operator for them. Withdrawing from the agent has a cost. A transfer to the wrong number is hard to recover, so check twice before confirming. And scams are numerous: “I sent you money by mistake, send it back to me,” or “I am from the operator, give me your code.” Do not respond, and always check your balance yourself, never from the other person’s message. For a business, a “merchant” account is often required, with the company’s papers.

Is my money protected?

In the countries of the West African Monetary Union, of which Benin is a part, there is a deposit guarantee fund. If an approved bank or microfinance institution goes bankrupt, this fund reimburses depositors, up to a limit set by the ministers of the Union. Ask your institution what this limit is today. This protection applies only to approved institutions: it does not cover unknown companies that promise huge gains.

No serious bank promises to double your money in a few weeks. “Investments” that promise huge and quick gains are often pyramids: the first are paid with the money of those who follow, then everything collapses. “One who is eager to be rich will not go unpunished” (Prov 28:20). We will talk about it again in Module 14.

An example (made-up story)

Mariam is a seamstress. Her clients pay when they can: sometimes a lot, sometimes nothing. She keeps everything in a box at home, and every time a relative has a problem, the box empties. She decides to open a savings account.

She visits two approved institutions. The first asks 1,500 F per month in account-keeping fees: that makes 18,000 F per year. The second asks 500 F per month: 6,000 F per year. The difference is 12,000 F every year, almost a week of her savings. She chooses the second, which is also closer to her workshop.

She deposits 5% of every payment received there, and keeps her Mobile Money number only for small expenses. After a few months, the box no longer empties and the account grows. (The figures are only there to give an example.)

My sheet: comparing two institutions

Go and see two institutions. Ask the questions and write down the answers.

My questionInstitution 1Institution 2
Name of the institution
Is it approved? (yes / no)
Distance from my home
Minimum deposit to open
Opening fees
Account-keeping fees (per month)
Price of the card
Withdrawal fees
Phone app? Link with Mobile Money?
Interest on savings
What I think of the welcome

To sum up

An account protects you from theft, from forgetfulness and from yourself. Always check that the institution is approved, ask for the list of fees in writing and compare before choosing. Never give your codes to anyone, and be wary of anyone who promises huge and quick gains.

lecons.titre: Mastering your money — Credit: understand well before borrowing
lecons.html:
Borrowing: a good or a bad thing?

“The rich rule over the poor. The borrower is servant to the lender” (Prov 22:7). “Owe no one anything, except to love one another” (Rom 13:8). The Bible warns us against debt. It does not say you must never borrow. It says: be careful, because debt chains you.

A loan is a promise. You promise someone to give money back later, with a supplement. You thus commit the money you will earn tomorrow, before having earned it. That is why you must count well beforehand: “For which of you, desiring to build a tower, doesn’t first sit down and count the cost, to see if he has enough to complete it?” (Luke 14:28).

There are two kinds of loans. The loan that produces: with this money, you buy a tool, stock, training, and it will bring you enough to repay, and even more. The loan that consumes: with this money, you eat, you party, you buy an item that brings in nothing. You will have to repay with tomorrow’s work, without earning anything extra.

Before signing, always ask yourself this question: will what I buy with this loan help me repay it? If the answer is no, think for a very long time.

The words to know

A lender who speaks with complicated words sometimes frightens you. Here is the essential:

The wordWhat it means
The principalThe sum you borrow.
The interestThe price you pay the lender for having used his money.
The rateThe interest expressed as a percentage. Beware: it can be per month or per year.
The termThe time you have to repay.
The installment (or due payment)The sum to pay at each date: per month, per week, etc.
The processing feesWhat the lender takes to study your application. They are often paid at the start, even if the loan is refused later.
The insuranceA protection that repays the loan in your place if you die or can no longer work. It has a cost.
The guarantee (or surety)What the lender can take if you do not pay: a property, a land title, or a person who commits to paying for you.
The deferralA delay at the beginning, during which you do not yet repay.
The late-payment penaltyA supplement to pay if you do not pay on the scheduled date.
The amortization scheduleThe list of all your payments: the date, the sum and the share of interest. Always ask for it.

Understanding the interest rate

Per month or per year?

A rate of 2% per month is not “only 2%.” It is 24% per year. To go from month to year, multiply by 12. So always ask: “Is this rate per month or per year?”

Calculated on what?

This is the most common trap. Two loans can announce the same rate and cost very differently, depending on how it is calculated. In the first case, the interest is calculated on the starting sum (we speak of a flat rate): you pay on the amount borrowed at the beginning, from the first to the last month, even when you have already repaid a large part of it. In the second, it is calculated on what remains to be repaid (declining rate): the interest goes down as you repay, since you owe less and less.

Example. You borrow 100,000 F for 10 months at 2% per month, repaying 10,000 F of principal each month.

• Interest calculated on the starting sum: 2,000 F × 10 months = 20,000 F.

• Interest calculated on what remains: 11,000 F in total.

Same announced rate, 9,000 F of difference. In the first case, the real rate is much higher than the one you were told.

The only question that matters: how much extra do I pay?

Forget percentages for a moment. Do this calculation:

Cost of the loan = everything I repay (fees, insurance, interest) − what I really received.

The smaller this figure, the better. Compare this figure from one offer to another.

The law sets a limit

In the countries of the West African Monetary Union, the law sets a maximum rate: the usury rate. A loan cannot cost more than this rate, all included (interest, fees, insurance). A decision taken at the end of 2025 set it at 14% per year for banks, and kept it at 24% per year for microfinance institutions and other lenders. These figures may change: ask for the limit in force on the day you borrow.

A private lender who asks you for 10% per month is not respecting the law. That is more than 120% per year. Do not fall into this trap, even if the need is pressing. It is the shortest path to ruin.

Where can you borrow?

WhereWhat is goodWhat is risky
The bankRates are generally the lowest. The rules are clear and supervised.It demands a lot: a regular income, often a salary that passes through it, guarantees. Delays are long.
MicrofinanceIt lends to people whom banks refuse. It accepts small amounts.Rates are generally higher. It often asks for savings first, or a group guarantee. Repayment is frequent (every week or every month).
Small loans on phoneVery fast. No paperwork.Fees are fixed and the term very short. Calculated over a year, they make a very high rate. It is easy to take another one to pay the first.
The tontine, the associationNo interest, or low interest. The rules are known to all.Everything rests on trust. A delay harms the whole group.
Family, friendsNo interest. You can speak frankly.An unpaid debt breaks a relationship. Always write down the sum and the repayment date.
The employer (salary advance)No or little interest.It reduces your salary of the following month. Do not repeat.
The private lenderHe gives quickly and without paperwork.Rates are often illegal. Threats and seizures are frequent. To be avoided.

For emergency cases, also speak to the Alliance: the Grace Fund, managed by the MBEL ministry, exists to help.

How to analyze a loan

Here is a method in six questions, to ask before signing. The first: what will this money be used for? Is it a loan that produces, or a loan that consumes? Second question: how much will you really receive? Often, processing fees, insurance or blocked savings are withheld. If you borrow 300,000 F and 3,000 F is withheld, you receive 297,000 F, not 300,000 F.

Third question: how much will you pay in total? Ask for the amortization schedule and do the calculation of the cost of the loan. Fourth: can you pay the installment even in a bad month? This is the most important question, and we will come to it in a moment. Fifth: what happens if you can no longer pay? Penalties, seizure of the guarantee, prosecution of the person who stood surety. Finally, have you compared at least two offers? A bank and a microfinance institution, or two microfinance institutions, on the sheet at the end of this part.

What installment can I bear?

Remember the two numbers we spoke about earlier: the minimum to live on and what you earn on average per month. What remains, after the minimum to live on, is the only sum with which you can repay a loan.

Simple rule: the total of all your installments (all your loans together) must not exceed one third of what you earn on average, nor what remains after your minimum to live on. Take the smaller of the two.

If your income is irregular, calculate with your bad months, not with the good ones.

An example (made-up story)

Koffi is a mechanic. He wants to buy a tool that costs 300,000 F. He can repay it in 12 months. He receives two offers.

The microfinance institution says: “Only 1% per month!” But this rate is calculated on the starting sum. There are 3,000 F of processing fees. Installment: 28,000 F. Total repaid: 339,000 F. Cost of the loan: 39,000 F.

The bank says: “13% per year.” This rate is calculated on what remains to be repaid. There are 3,000 F of processing fees. Installment: about 26,800 F. Total repaid: about 324,500 F. Cost of the loan: about 24,500 F.

The microfinance’s “1% per month” looks smaller than the bank’s “13% per year.” But it costs about 14,500 F more, because it is calculated on the starting sum. Koffi did the calculation before signing. He chose the bank, because it accepts his account opened a year ago. (The figures are only there to give an example.)

The main types of loans

The loanWhat it is for
The cash-flow loan (or working capital)Buying stock, paying current expenses, while waiting for clients’ payments. To be repaid quickly.
The equipment loanBuying a machine, a tool, a work vehicle. The term is longer.
The microcreditA small loan, often to people who are starting or growing a small activity. It can be individual or in a group (joint guarantee).
The consumer loanBuying a household item, a phone, furniture. It brings in nothing. To be handled with caution.
The school loanPaying the costs of training or studies.
The real-estate loanBuying or building a house, a plot of land. Large sums, long terms, heavy guarantees.
The overdraftA loan that arrives without being asked for, when the account is empty (see below).

The overdraft: the loan you do not see

An overdraft is when you spend more money than you have in your account and the bank accepts anyway. You have 20,000 F in your account. You pay 35,000 F with your card. The bank pays the difference in your place, and your account shows minus 15,000 F. These 15,000 F are money the bank has lent you, without your having signed anything that day.

This loan is not free. The bank charges interest (called “overdraft charges”), calculated every day as long as the account stays negative, and often additional commissions. It is one of the most expensive forms of credit. And it can become a habit: the salary arrives, the bank first takes back what it advanced, the account is empty from the start of the month, and you fall back into overdraft. It is a circle.

Two cases must be distinguished. The authorized overdraft is agreed with the bank, with a known limit and price: it is a loan, to be used very rarely. The unauthorized overdraft happens when you exceed what is allowed. The fees are then heavier, and the bank can refuse payments or take your checkbook away. The rule: follow your balance, do not spend more than you have, and if an overdraft happens, bring the account back to zero as soon as possible.

When you should not borrow

There are moments when the best decision is not to sign. To eat or pay the rent, except in a real emergency (we spoke earlier about the last-resort loan). To repay another loan: a loan that pays a loan is a trap. For an “investment” that promises huge gains: you borrow money that you risk losing forever. To keep up appearances, with a party, an overly expensive wedding, a garment or a phone to impress. When the installment exceeds a third of your income. And every time you have not read or not understood the contract: never sign what you do not understand.

Standing surety for someone

A friend or relative asks you to “sign” for him. By signing as guarantor, you tell the lender: “If this person does not pay, I will pay.” The day the other no longer pays, the lender will come to see you, not him.

The Bible warns us clearly on this point (Prov 6:1-5; Prov 22:26-27). The rule is simple: stand surety only for a sum you are ready to lose, without resenting anyone. When in doubt, help in another way, for example with a small gift.

If I can no longer pay

Above all, do not disappear. Go and see the lender before the missed date, tell him the truth and propose a new schedule: many prefer an agreement to an unpaid debt. Ask for this agreement in writing, because an oral promise is worth little on the day of a dispute. Do not pay one loan with another loan. Also speak to the Alliance, because the Grace Fund is there for emergency situations. Cut non-obligatory expenses and look at what you can sell, as we saw for “the difficult month.”

My sheet: I analyze my loan

Fill in this sheet with two offers before deciding. If you cannot fill in a line, it means you must ask the lender the question.

My questionOffer 1Offer 2
Who is lending to me?
Sum I am asking for
Sum I really receive (after fees withheld)
Term of the loan
Rate (per month or per year?)
Calculated on the starting sum or on what remains?
Processing fees, insurance, blocked savings
My installment
Total I will repay
Cost of the loan (total repaid − sum received)
Guarantee or surety requested
Penalty in case of delay
Is my installment under a third of my income, and under what remains after my minimum to live on?

To sum up

A loan is a promise on your money of tomorrow: count before signing. Always ask whether the rate is per month or per year, and on what it is calculated. The only figure that matters is the cost of the loan, what you will repay minus what you received. Your installment must stay under a third of your income, and under what remains after your minimum to live on. Avoid the overdraft, stand surety only for what you can lose, and if you can no longer pay, speak early to the lender and to the Alliance.

lecons.titre: Mastering your money — Savings and protection
lecons.html:
Why save?

“There is precious treasure and oil in the dwelling of the wise; but a foolish man swallows it up” (Prov 21:20). Joseph did not wait for the famine to act. He set aside during the seven years of abundance (Gen 41:34-36). Saving is not a lack of faith. It is wisdom: you prepare for the difficult day while the day is good.

Savings protect you when a blow comes: an illness, a breakdown, the loss of a job. They spare you debt, because without them, every problem becomes a loan. And they allow you to move forward: buy a tool, pay for training, launch a project, without borrowing.

Remember the rule we saw: pay yourself first. You do not save “what is left” at the end of the month, because nothing is ever left. You first set aside, then you live on the rest.

Three kinds of savings

Not all savings are made for the same thing. Separate them, with a name and a goal for each.

Kind of savingsWhat it is forWhere to keep it
Emergency savingsUnforeseen hard blows: illness, breakdown, job loss.A savings account where you can take the money back quickly, but without a card, so as not to touch it by reflex.
Project savings (six months to three years)A specific goal: a tool, training, an advance on rent, a family celebration.A savings account, or an approved microfinance fund. A term account if you are sure of the date.
Long-term savingsThe future: land, house, retirement, children’s studies.Investments designed to last (we will discuss them in Module 14).

Emergency savings: the first to build

This is the one that spares you from borrowing on the day everything goes wrong. Start with it, before any other project. We have already spoken about your minimum to live on. Here are the levels to reach, one after the other:

LevelExample if the minimum to live on is 80,000 FWhat it gives you
One week of the minimum to live on20,000 FThe first small shock no longer knocks you down.
One month80,000 FYou hold on for a month without income.
Three months240,000 FYou can look for a job or repair things without panic.
Six months (if your income is irregular)480,000 FA real safety cushion.

(The figures are only there to give an example. Do the calculation with your own minimum to live on.)

This savings is touched only for a real emergency. Before touching it, ask yourself three questions: is it unforeseen? is it urgent? is it necessary? An illness, an indispensable repair, a death: yes. A promotion, a party, a purchase to impress: no. And if you touch it, rebuild it before resuming your other projects.

How to save when it is hard

Set a percentage rather than a remainder: 5% or 10% of every sum received. Even a very small sum, if regular, is worth more than a large sum just once. And save on the day the money arrives, that very evening, not the week after. If possible, ask for an automatic transfer to your savings account.

Then put a little distance: an account without a card, or in a different institution from the one for your expenses. Give a name to each sum, “Emergency,” “Work tool,” “Training”: it is hard to touch a sum that has a name. Write your goal with an amount and a date. “240,000 F by the end of December” is a goal; “I would like to save” is not.

Saving with others also helps: a small savings tontine with trusted people forces you to hold on. And when you reach a level, celebrate it without spending the sum. A small thanksgiving, a simple meal with the family.

When your income is irregular, save more in the good months. It is in the good months that you prepare for the bad ones. Never count on a good month to cover a future month.

Savings are not investment

Many people mix the two. They are two different things:

SavingsInvestment
The goalSafety and availability.Making your money grow.
The riskVery low.More or less high. You can lose.
Is the money available?Yes, quickly.Not always. Sometimes locked or hard to sell.
What it earnsLittle.More, but without guarantee.

The rule: emergency savings first, investment afterward. Investing money you might need tomorrow is putting yourself in danger.

Inflation: why idle money loses value

Inflation is when prices rise over time. With 1,000 F, you bought more yesterday than today. Your money has not disappeared, but it buys less.

Example. Imagine prices rise by 3% per year.

• What costs 100,000 F today will cost about 134,000 F in ten years.

• If you keep 100,000 F in a box for ten years, you will still have 100,000 F… but it will buy only what is bought today with about 74,000 F.

In recent years, in Benin, prices have risen moderately, on average between 1% and 3% per year. But the prices of basic products, such as food or fuel, move much more from one month to the next. And in 2008, inflation exceeded 15%. Inflation can return, and it gives no warning.

Savings protect you from hard blows, but they do not make your money grow. For it to keep its value over long years, you will also need to invest part of what you have. That is the subject of Module 14.

The power of time

The earlier you start, the more you gain, even with small sums. Imagine you set aside 10,000 F per month, in an account that would pay you 4% interest per year (this rate is an example: ask for your institution’s).

DurationWhat you have depositedWhat you have at the end
10 years1,200,000 Fabout 1,470,000 F
20 years2,400,000 Fabout 3,670,000 F

The interest itself produces interest: this is called compound interest. After twenty years, more than 1,270,000 F comes from time, not from your work. Time works for you, if you let it.

Insurance: protecting yourself from big blows

Savings cover small and medium blows. But a serious accident, a long illness, a fire or a death can cost millions, and no savings are enough. That is where insurance comes in.

“A prudent man sees danger and hides himself; but the simple pass on, and suffer for it” (Prov 22:3). “If anyone doesn’t provide for his own, and especially his own household, he has denied the faith” (1 Tim 5:8). Taking out insurance is not a lack of faith. It is taking care of those who depend on you.

How it works

You pay a small regular sum, the premium. In exchange, if misfortune strikes (the claim), the company pays all or part of the cost. Several people pay so that those who suffer misfortune are helped.

The wordWhat it means
The premiumWhat you pay, every month or every year.
The claimThe event that happened: accident, illness, fire, death.
The exclusionsWhat is not covered. To be read with the greatest care.
The deductibleThe part of the costs you pay yourself, even if you are insured.
The waiting periodThe time, after signing, before the insurance starts to apply.

Useful insurances

The insuranceIt protects againstGood to know
HealthThe costs of care, hospital, medicines.In Benin, the State has set up the ARCH program, with a health insurance component, and recent texts make basic health insurance mandatory. Inquire at your town hall or the national agency in charge of social protection to know what you are entitled to.
Life or deathThe loss of an income if the head of the family dies. Funeral costs.Useful as soon as people depend on you. Loans often have a linked death insurance.
Vehicle (third-party liability)The damage you cause to others with your vehicle.Mandatory for every motor vehicle. For a motorbike-taxi driver, it is vital.
HomeFire, flood, theft in the house.Especially important if you are an owner or if the house contains your work tools.
Activity or goodsFire, theft, or losses for your workshop, your shop, your stock, or sometimes your harvest.Ask whether your institution or the microfinance institution offers small suitable insurances (called “micro-insurance”).

Choosing your insurance well

Go through an approved company, and ask to see its approval. Be wary of an “agent” who has neither papers nor an office. Read the exclusions: many disappointments come from what was not read. Pay your premiums on time, otherwise the contract may be suspended and, at the moment of misfortune, you will not be covered. Keep the contract, with a copy, in a safe place, and tell a relative where it is. If a claim occurs, notify quickly, in writing, and keep all the evidence.

Above all, insure what you could not replace with your savings. No need to insure a small item. On the other hand, insure what would ruin you if you lost it.

Warning. Insurance is not an investment. Someone who sells you insurance by promising quick gains or “double your money” is deceiving you. Ask in writing what the product guarantees and what it costs.

Protecting your papers and your family

Keep your important papers in a safe place: birth certificate, land title, contracts, health booklets, insurance papers. Make copies, and store them elsewhere. Tell a trusted person where your accounts and papers are: if you are ill or if you die, your family must not have to search for everything in the dark. And do not leave them in the dark about what belongs to you, nor about what you owe. Inheritance disputes almost always arise from a lack of clarity.

An example (made-up story)

Hervé is a motorbike-taxi driver. His income changes every day. His minimum to live on is 90,000 F per month. He decides to build his emergency savings: he puts 10% of his earnings every evening into a savings account without a card, near the market.

After six months, he has the equivalent of one month of minimum to live on. One morning, his motorbike breaks down: a repair of 45,000 F. Before, he would have borrowed from a lender at 10% per month. This time, he pays with his savings and rebuilds the sum in three weeks.

He also took out the mandatory insurance for his motorbike, and he inquired about health insurance for himself and his family. He sleeps better. (The figures are only there to give an example.)
